definition: showing rude or arrogant lack of respect
memoryTip: In-solent: so rude you feel the insult — cheeky disrespect.
correctPassage: The student gave an insolent answer that left the principal speechless.
wrongPassages: Teachers praised her insolent manners for being perfectly polite all semester.
Please insolent the chairs into rows.
City hall issued an insolent license for shoe size only.

definition: the process of spreading more widely
memoryTip: Diffuse = scatter: ideas or particles spreading out.
correctPassage: The diffusion of new teaching methods reached rural schools within a year.
wrongPassages: The diffusion of the crowd into one tiny room made movement impossible.
She practiced diffusion by locking every window against the wind.
The museum's diffusion of the statue kept it sealed in a vault.

memoryTip: Ex tempore = out of the moment — no notes, no rehearsal.
correctPassage: When the slides failed, she delivered an extemporaneous talk that still won the room.
wrongPassages: His extemporaneous speech had been rehearsed for three solid weeks.
They filed an extemporaneous report after months of careful drafting.
The extemporaneous ceremony followed a script printed the day before.

definition: tending to remind one of something
memoryTip: Reminisce = remember: reminiscent things spark old memories.
correctPassage: The alley was reminiscent of the neighborhood where she grew up.
wrongPassages: The brand-new design was reminiscent of nothing anyone had ever seen.
He stayed reminiscent so he would never look back on the past.
A totally blank memory made the photo feel deeply reminiscent.

memoryTip: Enemy + -ity: the state of being someone's enemy.
correctPassage: Decades of enmity made even a handshake between the leaders unlikely.
wrongPassages: Their lifelong enmity was the reason they never stopped helping each other.
The club's enmity toward new members showed in warm welcome dinners.
She felt only enmity for the friend who had always stood by her.
